== Biography ==

'''John Glasgw''' was alive on '''2 March 1479/80''' and was already an adult witness in 1475. The conventional working birth estimate of about '''1450''' assumes he was a young adult at that first appearance; he could have been substantially older. No birth or baptism record is known.

John belonged to Stirling's late-medieval burgh community. He is assigned three property-record appearances: 11 April and 8 August 1475, and 2 March 1479/80. The official description of the August charter groups him with its burgess witnesses. The repeated uncommon name, town and witnessing role make these appearances very likely to concern the same man. None names his trade, wife or parents; burgess status is now attested in the August catalogue description.

The earlier Glasgow burgess known as '''John de Glasgu I''' may have been this John's father or another close relative. A single man could have witnessed acts from 1447 to 1480: a birth before about 1426 would make him at least about 54 in 1480. The conventional circa-1450 estimate inferred from adult witnessing in 1475 is not evidence against an older birth. Identity with the earlier burgess remains a viable alternative to a father–son or other close-family relationship; those alternatives must not be combined into one asserted pedigree.

=== Life in Stirling, 1475–1479/80 ===

==== 11 April 1475 ====

Robert Gelis, elder, and John Gelis, younger, sold Sir John Hastings, canon of Dunblane, an annual rent of 6s from a tenement on the north side of Stirling High Street. The property lay between the land of John Kyrkwoud on the west and that of the late Robert Haket on the east.

'''John Glasgw''' appears among the witnesses, together with burgesses, craftsmen, a chaplain and a notary public.<ref name="StirlingJohn">''Charters and Other Documents Relating to the Royal Burgh of Stirling, A.D. 1124–1705'' (Glasgow, 1884), abstracts dated 11 April 1475 and 2 March 1479/80; [https://archive.org/details/chartersotherdoc00stir Internet Archive].</ref>

The record places him in a formal property transaction in Stirling's market centre. It does not state his occupation, residence, burgess status or relationship to another bearer of the name.

==== 8 August 1475: a burgess witness ====

The official archive description of '''B66/25/43''', a charter granting parts of the Dow Croft and two rigs at Stirling, lists '''John Glesgw''' within its group of burgess witnesses. This is a further occurrence beside the two printed abstracts, and the clearest located evidence of his civic status. The nearby list includes John Brady and John Watsoun; the catalogue names no relationship between them and John Glesgw.<ref name="Stirling1475August">National Records of Scotland online catalogue, [https://catalogue.nrscotland.gov.uk/nrsonlinecatalogue/details.aspx?df=&di=y&dt=&k=holme&ko=a&r=&reference=B66%2F25%2F43&ro=s&st=1&tc=y&tl=n&tn=n&tp=n B66/25/43], charter dated 8 August 1475, held by Stirling Council Archives Services; official description inspected 15 October 2026. The description groups John Glesgw with the burgess witnesses. The original charter has not been inspected.</ref>

The surviving seals are attributed to bailie John Forester and burgess James Redhucht, not to John Glesgw. They cannot be used as his personal seal evidence. This remains a catalogue-level reading pending the original. It adds civic status, not a father, child or property owned by John.

==== 2 March 1479/80 ====

Adam Cosour resigned annual rents totalling 40s for the support of the altars of St Anne and the Virgin Mary in the parish church of the Holy Cross of Stirling.

The rents came from several Stirling properties, including:

* a tenement between the lands of Gilbert Brady and the late William Murray of Tulchadam;
* Duncan Thomson's tenement near the Friars;
* and the Trone land on the west side of the High Street leading to the burgh port.

'''John Glasgw''' again appears as a witness, with Thomas Stewart, Andrew Morys and others.<ref name="StirlingJohn" />

The repeated name and role, only four years apart, make it highly likely that the records concern the same man.

=== Documentary setting ===

The 1479/80 act appears to survive in the protocol book of '''James Darow''', chaplain and notary. Stirling Council Archives identifies Darow's 1469–1484 volume as the oldest surviving Scottish protocol book and gives the reference '''B66/1/1/1'''.<ref name="Darow">Stirling Council Archives, “Lawsuits and murder: the protocol book of James Darow, 1469–1484”; [https://www.stirlingarchives.scot/2015/07/17/lawsuits-murder-protocol-book-james-darow-1469-1484/ archive article].</ref>

The published Stirling texts are English abstracts rather than full diplomatic transcriptions. The apparent absence of ''de'' cannot therefore be treated as proof that the surname had become fixed. Inspection of the original may reveal the unmodernised name form, status omitted from the abstract, the complete witness list or further appearances in neighbouring entries.

=== Possible origin in the Glasgow burgess family ===

A close relationship to the earlier Glasgow burgess is plausible because:

* ''Johannes de Glasgu'' and John Glasgw are compatible forms;
* the chronology is possible;
* both clusters involve formal burgh property transactions;
* and no contradictory office, relationship or date is known.

It is not proved because:

* no witness or associate currently appears in both cities;
* no shared property is known;
* no trade, wife, child, parent or sibling is named; the August 1475 description does attest burgess status;
* no seal or signature is known;
* and no intervening record has been found between 1455 and 1475.

Separate record-group accounts remain useful while identity is tested. Their estimated birth years cannot establish two generations: a single man across 1447–1480, or two related men, are both viable working explanations.

=== Possible son and descendants ===

The leading family hypothesis makes [[Space:John_de_Glasgow_alias_Smith_/_John_Glasgow_of_Saltmarket'|John Glasgow of Saltmarket]] the son of the Stirling witness. John of Stirling was already an adult in 1475. The Saltmarket John is securely located in 1527; the circa-1480 birth estimate depends on the separate, unproved identification with John alias Smith in 1506. Neither that date nor two distinct father–son generations is established by the witnessing records.

The hypothesis is strengthened by the uncommon surname, consecutive generations and both men's participation in burgh property networks. Gilbert Brady's property in the 1479/80 Stirling act and the later Brade association in [[Glasgow-1098|William Glasgow]]'s household provide an additional surname-network clue. If the reconstruction is right, the Stirling John was probably William's grandfather.

No surviving act names the Saltmarket John as his son, so the relationship remains a working pedigree rather than a documented descent.

=== 5. Contemporary surname bearer: Alan Glasgw ===

A royal justice record dated 26 February 1494/95 refers to the '''slaughter of Alan Glasgw'''.<ref name="Alan1495">Robert Pitcairn, ed., ''Ancient Criminal Trials in Scotland'', proceedings dated 26 February 1494/95; [https://archive.org/details/criminaltrialsin01pitc Internet Archive].</ref>

Alan was dead by that date. His shortened surname form resembles the Stirling abstracts, but no relationship to John is known. The earlier assessment left him unplaced; the selected low-confidence son model below now supplies a revisable local placement.

=== 6. Incorrect Robert relationship ===

The 1475 charter does not name a Robert Glasgow who could be John's brother.

The Roberts belonged to the '''Gelis''' family: Robert Gelis, elder, the grantor, and his deceased father, also Robert Gelis. No Robert Glasgw appears in the cited witness list.

=== Evidence assessment ===

The secure evidence establishes that:

* John Glasgw/Glesgw is assigned three Stirling appearances in 1475 and 1479/80, including a burgess-witness group in the 8 August charter description;
* the compatible name variants, dates and civic setting very probably concern one man;
* he participated in formal property and religious-endowment business in the burgh;
* burgess status is attested by the August archive description; no trade, family relationship or property ownership is stated for him.

The evidence does not establish that he was the Glasgow burgess of 1447–1455, father of Alias Smith or William Glasgow, related to Alan Glasgw, or ancestor of the later burgh family.

=== Timeline summary ===

* '''about 1450''' — estimated birth based on adult witnessing in 1475
* '''11 April 1475''' — witnesses a Stirling High Street property transaction
* '''8 August 1475''' — John Glesgw is grouped among burgess witnesses in B66/25/43
* '''2 March 1479/80''' — witnesses a Stirling religious endowment involving several burgh rents
* '''26 February 1494/95''' — Alan Glasgw is recorded as slain; no relationship proved

'''Source-described occurrences assigned to John Glasgw of Stirling:''' 3 (two printed abstracts and one official charter description; originals still to inspect).

== For further research ==

* Inspect James Darow's protocol book, B66/1/1/1, for the full 1479/80 entry and neighbouring references.
* Inspect the 11 April 1475 act and the newly specified 8 August charter, B66/25/43, preserving their separate dates and witness lists.
* Search Stirling burgess rolls, court books and property records for Glasgu, Glasgw and variants.
* Reconstruct Gilbert Brady's property and family and test any relationship to the Glasgow Brade network.
* Search for explicit ''filius'', ''heres'', ''frater'', ''nepos'', ''relicta'' or succession clauses connecting John to later bearers.
* Keep the relationship to John de Glasgu I, Alias Smith and William Glasgow hypothetical until direct evidence appears.

== Selected working family — 15 October 2026 ==

The local family tree now selects '''John Glasgw of Stirling''' as an '''uncertain''' father of two compatible later bearers. This is an explicit working pedigree, not a newly found parent record.

* '''Saltmarket John''', provisionally represented by [[Glasgow-1095]], is the stronger existing father hypothesis: adult Stirling activity by 1475, compatible consecutive generations and burgh-property networks. The Brady/Brade association is a weak supporting clue. The imported profile mixes identities and may instead represent Stirling John; that alternative collapses this father link.
* '''[[Glasgow-3023|Alan Glasgw]]''' is selected more tentatively as a son from the existing son/brother/nephew comparison. His age and home are unknown. Jedburgh is the court venue, not his residence. Brother, nephew or another early family remain viable.

No mother or unnamed intermediary is invented. The identity of Stirling John with the Glasgow burgess of 1447–1455, or a father–son relationship between them, remains an '''unselected alternative'''; these models are not combined. Alan’s printed 1494/95 and regnal-year discrepancy still needs JC1/1 collation.

Sources remain the separately cited Stirling abstracts of 11 April 1475 and 2 March 1479/80, NRS B66/25/43 (8 August 1475), the Saltmarket title reconstruction of 1527–1553, and Pitcairn, ''Criminal Trials'' I, part I, p.19. No new original inspection is claimed. [https://glasgow.phenotype.dev/branches/early-scottish-records/#stirling-working-family Reasons, alternatives and the selected local tree].
